media_work.title: A False Report: A True Story of Rape in America
media_work.creator_name: T. Christian Miller and Ken Armstrong
media_work.focus_or_theme: Investigation of false rape accusations, victim credibility, police investigation methods
media_work.key_statistics: The book discusses statistics on rape victims and the prevalence of skepticism toward rape accusations

key_quotes_raw: The book highlights the dismaying skepticism and credibility issues surrounding rape accusers
systemic_issues_raw: Inadequate training in trauma-informed interviewing techniques
Lack of coordination between police departments in different jurisdictions
Tendency to disbelieve victims with complicated backgrounds or inconsistent accounts
policy_recommendations_raw: Better training for police in handling sexual assault cases
Improved coordination between law enforcement agencies
More trauma-informed approaches to interviewing victims
additional_resources_raw: The original ProPublica/Marshall Project article "An Unbelievable Story of Rape" that won the 2016 Pulitzer Prize
Netflix adaptation "Unbelievable" based on the same case
media_item.item_title: Book Content: A False Report: A True Story of Rape in America
media_item.focus_or_theme: Investigation of false rape accusations, victim credibility, police investigation methods
media_item.summary_notes: The book follows two parallel narratives: Marie Adler's experience being disbelieved and charged with filing a false report after being raped, and the later investigation by two female detectives in Colorado who connected multiple rape cases and eventually identified Marc O'Leary as the serial rapist responsible.  While not a traditional wrongful conviction case, it highlights similar systemic issues such as skepticism toward certain types of witnesses, pressure to close cases quickly, and the devastating impact of being disbelieved by the justice system. The book was expanded from a Pulitzer Prize-winning ProPublica/Marshall Project article.
media_item.case_details_raw: Marie Adler was wrongfully accused of filing a false police report after being raped.  Police pressured her to recant her allegation.  Marc O'Leary, an army veteran, was later identified as the serial rapist responsible for Marie's rape and others. He was arrested in 2011 and sentenced to 327.5 years in prison.

featured_individuals.sentence: Probation, court fees, and mandatory counseling
contributing_factors_raw: Inconsistencies in her account due to trauma
Lack of support system (foster care background)
featured_individuals.status_raw: Exonerated when her rapist was caught and confessed
organizations_involved_raw: Colorado detectives who solved the case
featured_individuals.cross_reference: This case was later adapted into the Netflix series "Unbelievable"
featured_individuals.individual_notes: 18-year-old at the time of the incident.

research_notes_raw:
This book is particularly relevant to wrongful conviction studies because it examines a case where the victim herself was wrongfully accused of a crime (filing a false report) when she was actually telling the truth. While not a traditional wrongful conviction case, it highlights similar systemic issues in the criminal justice system: skepticism toward certain types of witnesses, pressure to close cases quickly, and the devastating impact of being disbelieved by the justice system.

The book was expanded from a ProPublica/Marshall Project article by the same authors that won the 2016 Pulitzer Prize for Explanatory Reporting.
